```{r options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, fig.align = "center",
                      dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 90)
```

A heterogeneous transition network is an estimate. Every edge weight is a
proportion computed from the sessions that happened to be observed, and
every centrality is a function of those proportions. Claims drawn from one
estimate, that a transition from a human request to an AI action is strong,
that one code is more central than another, or that the AI hands back to the
human more often than it continues on its own, rest on the assumption that
another sample of sessions would give a similar network. Model assessment
quantifies how far that assumption holds before the network is used as
evidence (Saqr et al., 2025).

The assessments answer different questions and sit at different levels of
the network. The bootstrap and its closed-form counterpart ask which
individual edges are estimated precisely enough to interpret. Split-half
reliability asks whether the network as a whole would be the same in another
half of the data. Case-dropping stability asks how many sessions can be lost
before the ordering of the edges or of the node centralities changes. A
fourth question, whether a first-order network is adequate at all, is the
subject of the [Markov-order adequacy](markov-order.html) guide. Every
function below takes an htna network or a grouped network, and every
result has a `plot()` method.

```{r package}
library(htna)
```

## Data

`human_ai` holds 429 sessions of human-AI pair programming coded into six
human and six AI codes; each row is one coded event.

- **Session**: `session_id`; the unit that is resampled, split and dropped.
- **Code**: `code`; the node of the network.
- **Actor type**: `actor_type`, `"Human"` or `"AI"`.
- **Order**: `order_in_session`; the position of the event in its session.

The network assessed throughout is the relative transition network of all
sessions.

```{r build}
data(human_ai)
net <- build_htna(human_ai, actor_type = "actor_type")
```

## Which edges are estimated precisely?

`bootstrap_htna()` resamples the 429 sessions with replacement, rebuilds the
network on every resample and summarizes the distribution of each edge
weight. Under the default stability test, an edge is significant when its
resampled weights stay within 75% to 125% of the observed weight often
enough for the p-value to fall below 0.05.

```{r bootstrap}
boot <- bootstrap_htna(net, iter = 200, seed = 1)
boot
```

Of the 135 non-zero edges, 64 are reproduced by the resamples within the
consistency range. The strongest edge, from the AI's `Delegate` to its own
`Plan`, has a bootstrap mean of 0.611 with a 95% interval from 0.546 to
0.673. The edge table, one row per edge, holds the interval and the
p-value of every edge.

```{r bootstrap-table}
head(summary(boot))
```

Weak edges fail the stability test even when they are clearly present: the
self-transition of `Ask` has a weight of 0.0182 and an interval from 0.0129
to 0.0242 that excludes zero, but its resampled weights leave the narrow
consistency range around such a small weight too often (p = 0.154). The
test asks whether a weight is reproduced, not whether it differs from
zero. `plot_htna_bootstrap()` draws the network with the edges that pass
the test.

```{r bootstrap-plot, fig.height = 5.5}
plot_htna_bootstrap(boot, display = "significant")
```

`certainty_htna()` derives the same quantities in closed form, from the
Dirichlet posterior of each row of transition counts, without resampling.

```{r certainty}
cert <- certainty_htna(net)
cert
```

The closed-form analysis marks 68 edges as certain, and its intervals for the
strongest edges are close to the bootstrap ones (0.600, from 0.543 to 0.656,
for `Delegate` to `Plan`). The two verdicts agree on most edges:

```{r certainty-agreement}
both <- merge(summary(boot), summary(cert), by = c("from", "to"))
xtabs(~ sig.x + sig.y, data = both)
```

Of the 135 edges, 61 pass both tests and 64 fail both; the 10 disagreements
are edges near the boundary of the consistency range. The closed-form
analysis treats every transition as independent and so ignores the nesting of
transitions in sessions, which the bootstrap respects; it is the faster
screen, and the bootstrap the analysis to report.

## Would another half of the data give the same network?

`reliability_htna()` splits the sessions at random into two halves 200 times,
estimates a network from each half, and compares the two networks.

```{r reliability}
rel <- reliability_htna(net, iter = 200, seed = 1)
rel
```

Two networks estimated from disjoint halves of the sessions correlate at
0.982 on average (SD 0.0047), and their edge weights differ by 0.0125 on
average. Even the largest difference between the halves, 0.0955 on average,
is small beside the strongest edges of around 0.4 to 0.6. The network as a
whole does not depend on which sessions were sampled.

```{r reliability-plot}
plot(rel)
```

## How many sessions can be lost before the edge ordering changes?

`casedrop_reliability_htna()` drops increasing proportions of the sessions,
from 10% to 90%, re-estimates the network and correlates its edge weights
with those of the full network (Spearman correlation, off-diagonal edges).
The case-dropping stability (CS) coefficient is the largest proportion that
can be dropped while the correlation stays above 0.7 in at least 95% of the
200 resamples per proportion (Epskamp et al., 2018).

```{r casedrop}
cd <- casedrop_reliability_htna(net, iter = 200, seed = 1)
cd
```

The CS coefficient is 0.90, the largest proportion tested: even with 90% of
the sessions dropped, the 125 off-diagonal edge weights correlate with
those of the full network at 0.912 on average. The ordering of the edges is
therefore stable well beyond the conventional criterion of 0.5.

```{r casedrop-plot}
plot(cd)
```

## Are the centrality rankings stable?

Analyses often interpret rankings of codes by centrality rather than single
edges. `centrality_stability_htna()` applies the case-dropping procedure to
the in-strength, out-strength and betweenness of the codes.

```{r centrality-stability}
cs <- centrality_stability_htna(net, iter = 200, seed = 1)
as.data.frame(cs)
```

All three measures reach the maximum CS coefficient of 0.9. The correlation
traces behind the coefficients show how much of that margin each measure
has:

```{r centrality-stability-table}
as.data.frame(cs, what = "correlations")
```

In-strength barely moves (a mean correlation of 0.981 with 90% of the
sessions dropped), out-strength falls to 0.924, and betweenness, which
depends on shortest paths and reacts to small changes in the weights, falls
to 0.888, with 97.5% of the resamples still above the threshold. All three
rankings are stable enough to report; betweenness is the one to read with
the most care.

```{r centrality-stability-plot, fig.height = 4.5}
plot(cs)
```

## Which assessment to use

| Question | Function | Criterion used here |
|---|---|---|
| Which edges are reproduced by resampling? | `bootstrap_htna()` | p < 0.05 under the stability test |
| The same, in closed form | `certainty_htna()` | interval within the consistency range |
| Is the whole network the same in another half of the data? | `reliability_htna()` | mean split-half correlation |
| How many sessions can be lost before the edge order changes? | `casedrop_reliability_htna()` | CS coefficient above 0.5 |
| Are centrality rankings stable? | `centrality_stability_htna()` | CS coefficient above 0.5 per measure |
| Is a first-order network adequate? | `markov_order_test_htna()` | see [Markov-order adequacy](markov-order.html) |

The assessments are complementary and are best reported together. In these
data every criterion is met: the network is reliable across halves, its
edge order and centrality rankings survive the loss of most sessions, and
about half of its edges are individually reproducible. For a grouped
network, every function returns one result per cohort; the
[Grouped heterogeneous transition networks](grouped.html) vignette shows
the grouped forms.
